Photo by Ousa Chea on UnsplashSomewhere in the last year, AI quietly stopped summarizing science and started doing it
There’s a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from being a third-year PhD student staring at a spectrometer readout at 2 a.m., trying to figure out why your protein won’t crystallize the way the literature says it should. I know because a friend of mine lived that exact scene for the better part of a year. She eventually solved it — but not by reading one more paper. She solved it by asking an AI system to cross-reference three hundred failed crystallization attempts buried in unpublished lab notebooks and flag the one variable nobody had bothered to control for. It took the system about four minutes.
That’s the part of the AI story that doesn’t get nearly enough attention. Everyone talks about chatbots writing emails or agents booking flights, and sure, that’s useful. But somewhere in the last year, AI quietly crossed a much stranger threshold: it stopped being a tool scientists use to read faster, and started being something closer to a colleague who proposes what to try next.
From summarizing to hypothesizing
The old pitch for AI in science was modest — help you find the paper, extract the table, maybe translate the methods section…
